## Review

<img src="https://octodex.github.com/images/chellocat.jpg" alt="Octocat celebrating your completed documentation" width="150" align="right">

_Congratulations! You've completed all eleven steps!_

You practiced headings, task lists, code samples, images, and LaTeX in `day-1.md`. You also built a README in `project-guide/README.md` that helps a new teammate:

- Understand the project's purpose, audience, and features.
- Find prerequisites, follow setup, and verify the result.
- Follow usage examples, compare expected output, and locate project files.
- Contribute a change, ask for help, and understand the MIT license.
- Troubleshoot a problem and review documentation for accuracy and accessibility.

Finally, you described your work in a pull request and merged it after validation.

### Put it into practice

Ask someone unfamiliar with your journal to follow the README. Record where they get stuck and improve those instructions. Automated checks verify required structure; reader feedback tells you whether the documentation works.

Your project README remains in `project-guide/README.md` because the exercise toolkit updates the root README. Adapt it for your next real project, put it at the root, and maintain it whenever behavior or setup changes. Keep only sections that are useful and accurate for that project.

### What's next?

- Review GitHub's [README guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes).
- Explore [mathematical expressions](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/working-with-advanced-formatting/writing-mathematical-expressions).
- Continue with another [GitHub Skills exercise](https://learn.github.com/skills).
